newsitem.title: USA: Calif. judge orders release of Orange Cty transcripts.
newsitem.headline: Calif. judge orders release of Orange Cty transcripts.

text.p: A California judge Wednesday ordered that sealed grand jury transcripts about Merrill Lynch and Co.'s role in the Orange County bankruptcy be immediately made public.
But within hours, a state appeals court granted Merrill Lynch's request for an emergency stay of the lower court's decision. Merrill Lynch asked for the stay to allow it to appeal the ruling.
Wallace Wade, an assistant district attorney for Orange County, said his office was starting to duplicate the transcripts for release when news of the stay came through.
Earlier, Orange County Superior Court Judge David Carter ordered "the immediate release of the transcripts and documents of the criminal investigation of Merrill Lynch."

"There is a compelling and fundamental right on behalf of all citizens to have access to vital information relating to the loss of over $1.67 billion of the public's monies," he said in a written ruling.
Merrill Lynch quickly filed a notice of appeal and asked for an emergency stay of the ruling.
Soon afterwards, a three-judge panel of the California Court of Appeal, 4th Appelate District, in Santa Ana granted the stay "pending further order of this court."
Orange County filed for bankruptcy in December 1994 after losing more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. The southern California county emerged from bankruptcy last year.
In June, Merrill Lynch settled with Orange County's district attorney for $30 million, ensuring that the brokerage giant and its employees would not face criminal charges.

Lawyers for Orange County and news organizations asked Carter to give them access to the sealed grand jury transcripts. County attorneys said the transcripts could bolster their $2 billion-plus lawsuit against Merrill Lynch.
The suit alleges Merrill Lynch sold Orange County risky securities in violation of the law. Merrill Lynch has denied any wrongdoing and is contesting the allegations in court.
County prosecutors and Merrill Lynch had argued that the transcripts should remain sealed because no indictments were returned by the grand jury.
In a court filing last month, Merrill Lynch asked Carter to keep the transcripts sealed to protect proprietary information about the company and safeguard the reputations of its employees.
But in a strongly-worded decision, Carter ruled that the public's right to know outweighed the concerns raised by Merrill Lynch and the district attorney.

"The public, our state and federal elected officials and the financial community must be allowed access to information that allows them to examine the events that led to the largest municipal bankruptcy in our nation's history," Carter said.

Noting that Merrill Lynch had paid $30 million under the settlement with Orange County's district attorney while denying any wrongdoing, Carter said, "Legal scholars cannot recall any other case where a law enforcement agency agreed to accept a civil fine to terminate a criminal investigation of this magnitude."
